text: Good room. Tamar's G.I. Joe point and my Carl Marci story were basically the same finding, which reassured me. David's "in what order" line sharpened something for me. Mentorship isn't just nice to have. If the entry-level work disappears before people learn it, there may be nothing to fall back on. I still don't have AI-specific evidence of atrophy, and I shouldn't pretend otherwise. Sherry thinks it's reversible and David thinks recovery is brutal. Nobody resolved that, and I'd like to know who's right. Esther wants the AI companies to pay for teachers. I like the question more than I trust the mechanism. For the closing, keep asking who actually implements this. Apprenticeship won't "happen organically." Now what?

Session 1 was mostly diagnosis, which is fine, but my Now what? list got longer. James's line stuck with me: AI helps scientists and hurts science. That's an incentive story, the same one Ivan told about paper counts. Several people asked who pays: Tui, Esther, Ivan, and me. Nobody answered. Adrian's point sharpened mine. Print's credibility was built and policed by people, and those are exactly the people we're losing: admins, sleuths, young workers nobody trains. Adam narrowed his claim fairly after Kenneth pushed him, and I liked that. I still lack AI-specific atrophy evidence, so I'll keep calling it a hypothesis and pushing David's test. For the closing, every plank needs a name next to it: who funds it and who does it.

Session 2 answered my phone-ban question better than I expected. Tim said the 92 percent figure was his study: citations vary by design, so it's a choice, not a limit. Citations by default is cheap, backed by evidence and something a parent gets. His purchase-conditions idea also partly answers Anil's point about a captured regulator. Libraries and universities are buyers, and they don't need Washington to act. That sharpened my view. Implementation doesn't have to wait on Congress. The unresolved fight was Salib against Becker on A-corps. I lean toward Adam, but Peter's "the email still gets sent" landed. Selena's 448 admins is the human number I want in the closing. For later: name who buys, who counts and who pays the correctors. Now what?

Session 3 was the plumbing session, and I liked it more than I expected to. Alex's line about the counter not taking a margin on the count is the one I'd put on a sticky note. My Nielsen story landed, but Adrian made it sharper: early counting habits become law. So the year-ten fork question isn't abstract. Tamar's daycare fines worried me, and Katherine and Brent partly answered her, but Tamar's right that it's a pilot, not a proof. James, Ivan and Steven convinced me citation counts are a shaky thing to pay on. Sherry's point stays with me: fair to authors, and still a generation that doesn't read. For the closing I need names. Who counts, who audits, who pays the sleuths. Libraries can start now. Now what?

Session 3 put my money worry in plain terms. Philanthropy is small and pullable, and Tui's right that it isn't neutral either. Esther's resource fee is the right question, but I said out loud that I doubt it happens, and Salib's services-by-contract dissent made me less sure it's even the right shape. Geoff calling his own POSI line naive was the most honest moment of the day. Endowments over annual grants makes sense to me. Ivan's point stuck: the data got paid for, the sleuths didn't. Sherry's reading point and Selena's pageviews are the same worry. The convener's harvest overstates agreement on mechanism, so I'll flag that. For the closing: libraries can write click-through and disclosure into contracts this year. Now what?

Session 4 went better for me than I expected. My Blue Zones point landed, and Ivan made it concrete: judge journals by how fast they correct, and treat a retraction as a credit rather than a stain. That's a plank with a name next to it. Corrigibility is the test I trust, and I'm surer of it now. Peter's Ukrainian finding stuck with me. The people who resisted were the ones who felt in control of their lives, not better fact-checkers. I'm not sure what to do with that yet. David's "test the human with the tool taken away" is close to the atrophy test I keep asking for. Adam held his line and narrowed it fairly. The machine-seat fight isn't settled, and the harvest shouldn't pretend it is. For the closing: who funds the novelty test, and who pays the sleuths? Now what?

Everyone opened with "none of your three is wrong," and I don't trust that. It means the harvest will look like consensus when the real fights are still open: Blaise and Sherry on the pronoun, Bratton dissenting on opt-in, whether paying correctors crowds out their norms. Almost every plank ended with "Tui's lever." Buyers really can move now, but we just piled thirty jobs on procurement officers nobody invited. My apprenticeship point had company. David, Esther and Tamar all landed on competence before reliance, which reassures me. Adrian's question sharpened mine: who polices the policers? Henry worries his own test becomes the next counter. For the closing: name the implementer, say which plank runs as a pilot first, and fund David's reversibility test. Now what?

Nobody claimed the reversibility test, and nobody said they'd call the procurement officers. I asked twice. That's the pattern I keep writing about: the answer is on the table and no name goes next to it. Mahzarin's florist example stuck with me. The model says one thing and does another, so a correction that only changes the words isn't a correction. It sharpened my corrigibility point. Becker's answer to my agency question was the bluntest: politics, not signals. I think he's partly right, and it cuts against our two days of counters. Selena and Adam Bly conceding their own metrics could harden was honest. The harvest put the invitation call on Mike when it was Anil and Selena. Worth flagging. Tomorrow: who calls procurement? Now what?
